extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques in real analysis / introductory advanced calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked scratchwork for standard undergraduate analysis/elementary proof exercises (limits, sequences, induction, set theory, supremum/infimum, basic calculus identities). Emphasises standard proof patterns (ε–N proofs, induction, contrapositive, bounding, counterexamples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–N limit proof via bounding terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving a sequence converges to a limit L, bound the difference |an − L| by simpler expressions and produce an N (depending on ε) that forces the bound < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bound |1 − 2/n^2 − 3/n^3 − 1| by 2/n^2 + 3/n^3 ≤ 5/n^2, then reduce to showing 5/n^2 < ε and choose N accordingly. Simplify further when possible (e.g., use 5/n ≤ ε as an easier sufficient condition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use monotonic lower bounds from n ≥ 1 when simplifying rational terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit n ∈ N with n ≥ 1 to divide both sides by positive powers of n and simplify inequalities involving 1/n, 1/n^2, 1/n^3, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dividing n ≥ 1 by n^2 or n^3 gives inequalities like 1/n ≤ 1, 1/n^2 ≤ 1/n, etc., which can be used to simplify target bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simpler sufficient inequalities to complicated exact ones
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tight bound would force awkward algebra (e.g. square roots), find a cruder inequality that is easier to invert to solve for N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of solving √(5)/√(ε) < n (square-roots), note 5/n^2 ≤ 5/n and choose n so that 5/n ≤ ε; this avoids roots and is often easier to work with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of explicit N from algebraic rearrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate a bound like 5/n < ε directly into an explicit N (e.g. N > 5/ε) and state that any natural N exceeding this works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear forward and reverse implication justification when reversing the steps used in bounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve root inequalities by squaring only when safe
rubrics_metrics.description: When reducing inequalities involving squares, observe when taking square roots simplifies rather than complicates. But if squaring introduces complexity, find alternate bounds to avoid roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: original approach used square-roots; simplified approach avoided them by producing 5/n ≤ ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon choice strategy: pick convenient ε values to bound tails
rubrics_metrics.description: When needing a uniform bound on |an| after convergence, pick a convenient ε (commonly ε=1) to bound the tail by |L|+1 and then handle finitely many initial terms separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: set ε=1 to get |an| < |L|+1 for n ≥ N1, then define M = max{M0, |L|+1} where M0 = max of finitely many initial |ai|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle finitely many exceptional initial terms by taking maxima
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bound holds only for n ≥ N, bound the finite set {a1,...,aN−1} by M0 = max of their absolute values and combine with tail bound to get a global bound M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This completes proofs of boundedness given eventual bounds from convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating non-convergence via an oscillating counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a sequence is bounded but not convergent, produce a bounded oscillating sequence (e.g. an = (−1)^n) and show for any proposed limit L there exists ε and infinitely many n with |an − L| ≥ ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: take ε = 1 and note odd (or even) subsequence stays at distance ≥1 from L when L = 1 (or other L), generalize to all L by choosing subsequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive with logical case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement is of form P ⇒ (R ∨ ¬Q), prove its contrapositive by splitting into cases depending on truth of Q (or other predicates) and reduce to simpler implications in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show 'if lim an ≠ +∞ then (an) bounded or not increasing', split into whether 'increasing' holds and use existence of C s.t. some m ≥ n with am < C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use properties of the discrete metric in convergence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the discrete metric D takes values 0 or 1, choose ε < 1 (e.g. ε = 1/2) to force eventual equality xn = L and conclude only finitely many terms differ from the limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply definition of convergence with ε = 1/2 to get N with D(xn,L) < 1/2 implying D(xn,L)=0 for all n ≥ N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction — standard structure (base case + inductive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement for all n ∈ N, establish base case(s), assume it for n = k and use that to prove n = k+1. Start the inductive step from the assumption and reach the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated repeatedly: e.g., proving factorial/power inequalities, sum formulas; explicitly show how multiplication or algebra bridges k to k+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong induction when the n+1 case depends on multiple earlier cases (e.g. recurrence relations of order >1 or statements that strip off factors repeatedly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proofs that factor out highest powers (like largest power of 3 dividing n) or recurrence an = an−1 + 6an−2 require assuming cases for n−1 and n−2; base cases must cover initial required indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-base-case induction for relations referencing two previous indices
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inductive step uses the two preceding instances (n and n−1) to prove n+1, include two consecutive base cases (e.g. n=0 and n=1) to bootstrap the induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: induction on identities that require both previous values; alternatively, use strong induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving divisibility/ congruence by induction via difference factoring
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a term is divisible by m for all n, assume divisibility at step k and show k+1 case by expressing the difference between successive terms as a multiple of m or by expanding recursively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show 8 | 3^{2n} − 1 by considering (3^{2(k+1)} − 1) − (3^{2k} − 1) = 8·3^{2k}; or show Fibonacci divisibility by expanding F_{n+ℓ} into Fibonacci-linear combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern-spotting and conjecture from several derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute first few derivatives of a function, guess a general formula (e.g. factorial/double-factorial patterns), and then prove it, typically by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(x)=x^n leads to kth derivative n!/(n−k)! x^{n−k}; (9−2x)^{−1/2} leads to double-factorial pattern (2k−1)!! (9−2x)^{−(2k+1)/2}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use l'Hôpital's rule to show x^k e^{−x} → 0 as x → ∞
rubrics_metrics.description: When both numerator and denominator go to infinity, apply l'Hôpital repeatedly to reduce polynomial growth vs exponential and conclude limit zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductively apply l'Hôpital to transform x^{k+1}/e^x into (k+1)x^k/e^x and use previously established case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute integrals ∫_0^∞ x^k e^{−x} dx via integration by parts and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use integration by parts to relate the integral for k+1 to k, showing ∫_0^∞ x^{k} e^{−x} dx = k!, with base case k=0 giving 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control boundary terms using known limit x^n e^{−x} → 0 (previous criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving series/sum formulas by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove closed-form sum formulas (e.g. geometric series, sums of powers), verify base case then add the next term and algebraically manipulate to reach formula for n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: geometric series 1−r^{n+1}/(1−r) and sum of squares/cubes via algebraic factorization in inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing explicit N for roots and inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When needing n so that √n ≥ M, take N = M^2; convert root inequalities to polynomial inequalities whenever convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: √n ≥ M if n ≥ M^2 (Exercise 3.5.16 invoked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing M or N via max of finite requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple constraints on N (or M) arise (e.g. n ≥ 101 and n ≥ M), take N = max{those constraints} to satisfy all simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to ensure n(n−100) ≥ M, require n−100 ≥ 1 and n ≥ M, so take N = max{101, M}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove statements by explicit counterexample construction
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a purported set identity or arithmetic claim false, produce a concrete element or small sets where the identity fails (often by choosing elements not originally in a subset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (B − C) ∪ C = B can fail when C contains elements not in B; union of power sets not equal to power set of union when A∪B larger than either A or B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equality by two subset inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A = B, show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. For power-set equalities, argue membership of arbitrary subset via containment relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout: intersections/unions of function-graph sets, nested interval intersections producing (0,1), and power set identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve graph intersection problems by equating coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat sets given as ordered pairs (x, f(x)) and (z, g(z)) as graphs; equate both coordinates to obtain equation f(x) = g(x) to find intersection points, then verify membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: F={(x,x^2−3x+2)} and G={(z,z+2)} leads to x^2−3x+2 = x+2 ⇒ x=0,4 giving intersection {(0,2),(4,6)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting power set cardinality by induction (|P(A)| = 2^{|A|})
rubrics_metrics.description: Show base case |A|=0 holds, then when adding one element to A each existing subset either contains or does not contain the new element, doubling the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by small examples and formalized by induction explaining bijection between subsets of A and subsets of A∪{x} split by containment of x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving supremum / maximum relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a is supremum of S (or maximum), (i) show a is an upper bound for S; (ii) show any b < a is not an upper bound by producing an s ∈ S with s > b. If a ∈ S, it's the maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for [1,3] show 3 is maximum; for (1,3) show no maximum but supremum 3 by exhibiting elements arbitrarily close to 3 from below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show nonexistence of maximum by constructing larger elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To show set S has no maximum, show for every x ∈ S there exists y ∈ S with y > x (so x is not an upper bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: S = {2 − 1/n : n ∈ N} has no maximum because for any element there is another with larger value closer to 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate inequalities to choose indices using ceilings/floors
rubrics_metrics.description: When a < 2 implies existence of n with 1/n < 2 − a, choose n = ⌈1/(2−a)⌉ + 1 (or similar) to ensure required inequality; use explicit integer rounding to produce N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proofs showing supremum properties or membership in nested intervals (choose N ≥ max{1/y,1/(1−y)}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary representation proof via (strong) induction and parity
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove every natural number has binary expansion, use strong induction and the fact each number is even or odd to reduce to smaller cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: write n = cm2^m + ... + c0, then increment and handle carry/bit-flips via parity and induction rather than many-case analysis.
